answer: Expose a batch endpoint that accepts many user IDs and returns each one's status (GET /status/users?ids=u1,u2,u3,u4). With a single-user endpoint, rendering four users takes four API calls — a poor experience and a burden on the backend; batch makes one network call and the backend does the heavy lifting.

answer: POST /heartbeat. Each client periodically calls it saying 'I am alive'; it marks whichever user is authenticated on the request as alive (updates that user's last heartbeat).
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'The endpoint is POST /heartbeat. Each call marks whichever user is authenticated on that request as alive.'

answer: A client can announce coming online but can't reliably announce going offline: a crash, dead battery or pulled plug sends no offline call, so the UI keeps showing the user online (stale dot). You aren't in control of the moment the device dies, so heartbeats must be periodic.
evidence: Ch2 §2.4: 'A client can announce coming online but can't reliably announce going offline: a crash, a dead battery or a pulled plug sends nothing... This fundamental limitation is why heartbeats must be periodic.'

answer: When the backend receives no heartbeat for 'long enough'. Long enough is subjective business logic/product decision configured per system (10 min, 10 s, a minute...); in this design 30 seconds of silence, with heartbeats every 10 seconds.
evidence: Ch2 §2.4: '"Long enough" is subjective... For one system it might be 10 minutes...; for others 10 seconds or a minute. This design marks a user offline after 30 seconds of silence, with clients sending a heartbeat every 10 seconds.'

answer: Instead of a boolean, store the time the last heartbeat was received: table pulse(user_id, last_heartbeat), stored as epoch seconds; every POST /heartbeat updates (upserts) that user's row.
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'instead of a boolean, store the time at which the last heartbeat was received. The table is pulse(user_id, last_heartbeat), and every POST /heartbeat updates that user's row.'

answer: No. Tables are only drawn to help you see a schema; they don't mean a relational database (model it however you want), and SQL is just an easy way to explain the idea.

answer: Rule 1: no entry for the user → offline (never came online). Rule 2: entry exists but last_heartbeat is older than now − 30 s → offline. Otherwise → online. Same rules for every ID in a batch call.
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'Rule 1: if there is no entry for a user, return offline... Rule 2: if there is an entry but its last_heartbeat is older than now minus 30 seconds... return offline. Otherwise the user is online.'

answer: Every 10 seconds.
evidence: Ch2 Fig 2·f: 'heartbeat every 10 s'.

answer: 8 bytes: two integers, a 4-byte user ID and a 4-byte last-heartbeat timestamp (raw payload; a real DB adds row overhead, e.g. ~36 bytes in PostgreSQL).

answer: The end user only sees online or offline, so treat absence of an entry as offline: a row exists only for online users. Each heartbeat resets a 30 s timer and entries are deleted when it runs out, so number of entries = users online at that moment, cutting rows significantly.
evidence: Ch2 §2.7: 'treat the absence of an entry as offline. A row exists only for a user who is online... The number of entries then equals the number of users online at that moment.'

answer: 100,000 entries, about 800 KB.

answer: A cron job that periodically scans the pulse table and deletes entries whose last heartbeat is older than 30 s (getStatus then = exists → online). Drawbacks: not robust, edge cases to handle; it adds another moving part — a separate process you must host, keep constantly running (or the business logic falters), whose uptime matters as much as the REST service's, plus monitoring and telemetry. Works for a just-launching startup.
evidence: Ch2 §2.7: 'The simplest answer is a cron job... That would work for a startup that is just launching. It is not a robust solution... The bigger cost is that a cron job adds another moving part... host it and keep it constantly running... monitoring and telemetry too.'

answer: Offload the expiry to the datastore: use a database with key-value access plus native expiration (TTL), instead of reinventing the wheel with a cron job. Named: Redis and DynamoDB.

answer: Each heartbeat sets the user's entry with a 30 s TTL, moving the expiration forward. After 30 s without a heartbeat the database deletes the entry itself. Entry exists → online; absent → offline. Caveats: in Redis the TTL must be re-sent on every write (plain SET clears it); in DynamoDB TTL deletes 'typically within a few days', so store expires_at and treat expires_at < now as offline.
evidence: Ch2 §2.8: 'On every heartbeat, set the user's entry... with a TTL of 30 seconds... every heartbeat moves the expiration time forward... If the entry exists, the user is online; if it doesn't, they are offline.' More precisely note.

answer: Five: three-way handshake to set up plus two-way teardown (database login and TLS come on top). The heartbeat write is a micro update (one row by primary key), so most of the time goes into establishing the connection, the biggest bottleneck; the database also spends CPU, bandwidth, buffers to accept each connection.
evidence: Ch4 §4.2: 'three-way handshake; closing it takes a two-way teardown... five network trips for every single call... most of the time goes into establishing the TCP connection, the biggest bottleneck in this design.'

answer: Keeping a set of connections open between the server and the database and reusing them (e.g. 3 created at startup); each query uses a free one, which goes back to the pool instead of being closed.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'Connection pooling means keeping a set of connections open between the server and the database and reusing them.'

answer: Because the database is spared the connection setup/teardown work (mainly CPU and network; memory too, per the note) — with one-row micro updates that work dominates, so load drops dramatically.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'the load on the database drops, even though the number of queries stays exactly the same. The database is spared the connection work, mainly CPU and network...'

answer: The API call becomes much faster (five trips saved; one request and one response), and the load on the database drops even with the same number of queries.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'That gives two benefits. The API call becomes much faster. And the load on the database drops...'

answer: Either it waits until a running query releases a connection, or the pool opens a new TCP connection, fires the query and adds it to the pool (3 → 4), up to the configured maximum; beyond the max, it waits (up to a timeout, e.g. HikariCP 30 s, then error).
evidence: Ch4 §4.5: 'the fourth request can wait until one of the three running queries releases its connection. Or it can establish a new TCP connection... and add that connection to the pool.'

answer: Max: stretching without a limit makes the pool grow unbounded with millions of requests, and every database has a limit on TCP connections — hundreds of servers × 100 connections is trouble. Idle TTL: close connections nobody uses (e.g. idle 10 min) so a server holds fewer connections on the database.
evidence: Ch4 §4.5: 'Stretching without a limit is a problem... Every database has a limit on the number of TCP connections it can hold... So the pool also closes connections nobody is using. You configure a TTL per connection.'

answer: No. It is a simple library running inside the API server process: at boot it creates connection objects in a blocking queue; a caller takes one (waiting if none free) and puts it back. (Central poolers like PgBouncer/RDS Proxy are separate services for a different problem.)
evidence: Ch4 §4.4: 'A connection pool is not one. It is a simple library running inside the api server... It is not a separate process.'

answer: Massive boost with micro updates (one row by primary key), where connection setup dominates. Outweighed when a big SQL query runs long enough (e.g. massive aggregations joining 10–15 tables) that query time exceeds connection setup.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'A big SQL query runs long enough to outweigh what the pool saves; the big win comes when updates are micro.' §4.6 on 10–15 table joins.

answer: Failure detection in a distributed system: nodes send heartbeats to a central server; a node whose heartbeats stop is down (e.g. your own AWS from EC2 machines, or your own load balancer detecting a down backend).

answer: The new server waits, retrying, and succeeds only when an existing server terminates one of its connections. It doesn't retry forever: the DB refuses extra connections with an error and the pool makes the caller wait only up to its timeout (30 s default in HikariCP), so requests on that server fail rather than hang. Fix: scale the database.
evidence: Ch4 §4.5: 'A new server waits, retrying, and succeeds only when an existing server terminates one of its connections. It does not retry forever...'

answer: The maximum number of connections it can handle. DB size depends on the concurrent queries you fire; the concurrency you want decides how many connections it must handle. To exceed the limit: scale vertically or shard.
evidence: Ch4 §4.6: 'Its size depends on the concurrent queries you fire at it... the most common bottleneck of a database in most cases is the maximum number of connections it can handle.'

answer: A small/lean team without ability to manage it should go for DynamoDB or another managed solution (managed Redis from Redis Labs/AWS/GCP if no expertise). Self-host Redis only when you have both the expertise and the engineering bandwidth; otherwise throw money at cloud providers.

answer: As taught: storage engines use B+ trees; a hard delete removes an entry from a node, imbalancing the tree, and the engine spends CPU rebalancing. A soft delete only updates the entry, so no rebalancing. Caveat: engines actually defer deletes (purge/VACUUM, merge only below 50% fill) and a soft delete is still a write, so the saving is smaller; choose soft delete for recovery/archival/audit, not as a B+ tree optimisation.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'easy on the database engine (no tree re-balancing)... With a soft delete, the entry is only updated and still exists, so the node doesn't need rebalancing.' More precisely note.

answer: VARCHAR (short text) stays inline with the other columns of the row. LONGTEXT is stored in a separate location on disk, with the row keeping only a reference; reading it takes two disk calls. (Engine details differ: InnoDB moves off-page only when the row is too long; PostgreSQL TOAST for wide values.)
evidence: Ch5 §5.6: 'A short text column (VARCHAR) stays inline... A long text column (LONGTEXT) is stored by the database in a separate location on disk..., and the row keeps only a reference to it.'

answer: Short text: bio (also email, first/last name). Long text: body (and long comments). Not everything inline because a row's length must be limited: gigantic text can't sit in rows, small rows scan easily (hard limits like InnoDB ~8 KB, MySQL 65,535-byte row). Keep the row to a bare minimum.
evidence: Ch5 §5.6: 'bio uses a short text type and body a long text type... Why not keep everything inline? A row's length has to be limited: gigantic text can't sit in rows, and small rows scan easily.'

answer: The engine serialises the date in some format; in a naive engine storing it as a string, every row's value must be read and converted back into a date-time object (extract date, month, year, hour, minute, second) before applying the comparison — expensive. How the DB stores it on disk determines performance. (Major engines actually use compact binary.)
evidence: Ch5 §5.7: 'The engine reads the string of every row, extracts date, month, year, hour, minute and second, and applies the comparison logic... how your database stores this data on disk determines its performance.'

answer: Convenient, sub-optimal, heavy on size and index.

answer: The number of seconds (or milliseconds) elapsed since 1 January 1970, stored in an integer column. As a string the date takes ~20 bytes; as epoch integer 4 bytes — 20 to 4, a massive gain (note: MySQL DATETIME is actually 5 bytes).
evidence: Ch5 §5.7: 'The epoch is the number of seconds, or milliseconds, elapsed since 1 January 1970... Stored as that string, the date takes about 20 bytes; as an epoch integer, 4.'

answer: You lose readability (can't tell the time from the number); also time zone information is somewhat lost, and the 4-byte int eventually overflows.
evidence: Ch5 §5.7: 'What you lose is readability.' §5.9: time zone somewhat lost in epoch; 4-byte int maxes out.

answer: Redbus had a table storing dates as date-time, and massive date-time comparisons made it the bottleneck (analytics-like use case). Epoch would cost readability (engineers read values in SQL IDEs/UI to debug). They needed only the date, not time, so relaxed that constraint and stored the date as an integer YYYYMMDD (e.g. 20220402): readable and fast integer comparison/index.
evidence: Ch5 §5.8: 'In 2016, Redbus... had a table storing dates as date-time, and massive date-time comparisons made it the bottleneck... They stored the date as an integer in YYYYMMDD form.'

answer: No. Both are integers and beat a slow native date-time; against each other there's no speed difference. YYYYMMDD buys readability, at the cost of inflexibility if time is needed.
evidence: Ch5 §5.8 Pause and think: 'against each other there's no speed difference... The custom format buys readability.'

answer: Time zone information. Handle it by keeping everything in UTC and rendering the epoch in the local device's time zone; if you need the original zone, store it in its own column.
evidence: Ch5 §5.9: 'A native date-time can capture time zone information, which is somewhat lost in the epoch... With an epoch, display is easy: render it in the local device's time zone... take everything in UTC.' Note: store zone in its own column.

answer: Not quite. Soft-deleted rows can be accumulated and hard deleted in one batch, clubbing the rebalancing (once or a few times, e.g. 100 rows per commit → 100× fewer rebalances) instead of per pointed delete. More precisely, batching mainly saves per-row transaction, locking and log overhead.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'Not quite... soft-deleted rows can be accumulated and hard deleted in one batch. Clubbing the deletes clubs the rebalancing.'

answer: The epoch keeps growing and will max out a 4-byte int (taught as 2032; actually 19 Jan 2038), forcing 64-bit, which doubles the space. Also pre-1970 dates need negative numbers. Recommended reading MySQL's official date-time documentation (not a blog/video/random person), explaining why MySQL serialises date-time instead of integers.
evidence: Ch5 §5.9: 'will max out a 4-byte int, forcing a move to 64 bits... So read MySQL's official date-time documentation, not a blog, a video or a random person.'

answer: Anything that helps you save a heavy computation or operation so you don't have to do it again: a result kept to refer to instead of redoing expensive computation, operation or I/O. Board: 'Caching: reduces response times by saving any heavy computation'.
evidence: Ch6 §6.1: 'Caching is anything, literally anything, that helps you save a heavy computation or a heavy operation so that you don't have to do it again.'

answer: No. Disk and network can be caches too: e.g. cache an expensive network call's result on the local disk and read it instead of making the call. Memoization and a database table are also caches.
evidence: Ch6 §6.1: 'Caches are not only RAM-based: you can use disk as a cache... If a network call is expensive, cache its result on the local disk.'

answer: Users → load balancer → three API servers; every API server has a line to one shared remote cache and to one database. The cache sits logically between API servers and database, physically a separate box; every server reads the same copy.
evidence: Ch6 §6.2 Fig 6·b: 'Three users send requests to a load balancer, which spreads them over three API servers. Every API server has its own line to one shared cache... and its own line to one database.'

evidence: Ch6 §6.2: 'Because the cache is remote, it doesn't matter which API server a request lands on... the load on the database drops by a massive margin.'

answer: First principles: connections (both persistent, cancel out); memory vs disk (Redis from RAM, DB worst case disk, though hot pages are in RAM); read size (tiny reads much faster in memory, ~1 KB minimal difference); storage structure (hash one shot vs B+ tree log n reads); cost and size (RAM costlier, limited). answer: Yes; a DB retention policy is a database thread running the cron job for you — offloaded. For performance, what always works: offload it to the database and stagger it. (MongoDB TTL task runs every 60 s; expiry can lag.)

answer: HTTP runs on top of TCP (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2), but there's no fixed tie: HTTP is a message specification, TCP a layer-4 protocol; in principle HTTP can go over UDP. HTTP needs a reliable ordered transport; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'HTTP runs on top of TCP... There is no fixed tie between them. HTTP is a specification for messages and TCP is a layer-4 protocol...'
